title: tmux inserts a black hole after emoji
body:
With tmux 3.5a running in GNOME Terminal 3.54.4 for GNOME 47 Using VTE version 0.78.4 +BIDI +GNUTLS +ICU +SYSTEMD, with Lynx 2.9.2 (using ncurses 6.5.20240629(wide)), when I call

> lynx https://<redacted-host>/s/0/e947872a-224b-4c84-8d25-90a541a9ec6-318.ics_en.html

it shows on the first line with the title an island with a black hole after it.  A picture for the black hole is

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/15fd426f-1e57-4b82-b572-f7eb26e958cf)

but this picture it is generated by loading the same file using emacs eww.  To utilize the latter, start emacs in text mode with `emacs -nw`, then press Alt-X, type `eww` ENTER, then type `https://<redacted-host>/s/0/e947872a-224b-4c84-8d25-90a541a9ec6-318.ics_en.html` and finally press once again enter.

The problem report is that when everything is tunnelled over tmux there is a black hole after the island emoji, which black hole is missing when tmux is not used.

Note that in this particular case after the island there is an explicit Unicode Variation Selector 16, which enforces colour presentation of the island. (as opposed to variation selector 15 for enforcing text mode of the emoji, or no variation selector for using some defaults).

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
From https://<redacted-host>/GNOME/vte/-/issues/2878:

> if they are displaying a character as width 2

tmux's developer misunderstood the situation, VTE does not display it as width 2. (If it did, it painted both cells with the desired blue background.)

Again, in VTE (and also in Xterm, which we usually consider the reference) the base character is of width 1 and VS16 does not make it wider. The base character + VS16 combined are altogether of width 1.

This is also what the standard libc methods `wcwidth()` and `wcswidth()` report, used by plenty of apps a libraries to compute the width occupied in a terminal (that's the very purpose of these methods).

I've already come across the concept of some terminals, breaking compatibility with others, somehow making them of width 2. I haven't seen a sort-of specification anywhere how this should exactly work wrt. subsequent overwrites, or at line break (when the increased width no longer fits in the line). Each terminal (tmux included) does what it thinks is the best with no cooperation or agreement whatsoever. Tmux could, as far as the behavior it shows towards the apps it hosts, pick any of these behaviors; bearing the consequences (corruptions) with apps that rely on `wc[s]width()` if it chooses to widen these characters; but towards its host terminal (VTE in this case) it's its job to know how the host behaves and implement the desired look on top of that platform.

"If VTE won't fix it", says tmux's developer over there. No, VTE is not broken here, it behaves the same way as Xterm, and the same way as dictated by `wc[s]width()`, which is a pretty damn reasonable behavior. We treat a base character + VS16 as having an overall width of 1. If someone thinks it's incorrect, they should please point us to relevant standards that say the width needs to be increased, give an exact specification how exactly to do that in the world of terminals in various corner cases outlined above, and give an answer how breaking the expected width as reported by `wcwidth()` and `wcswidth()` wouldn't cause a plethora of problems with various apps out there.

Until the world comes to an agreement that the width needs to be increased, comes up with an exact specification how this needs to be done, and figures out a solution to the `wc[s]width()` discrepancy this decision would cause, VTE's behavior is correct. Tmux needs to tolerate this behavior. If not for VTE, since apparently tmux's author doesn't care about VTE, then for Alacritty, Mlterm, Putty, St, Terminology, Xterm, Urxvt, Zutty, and presumably quite a few more, which also behave this way.

(By the way, this has already been discussed somewhere in VTE's or GNOME Terminal's issue tracker, possibly multiple times. I'm lazy to look it up, sorry.)

---
And to clarify one thing that I forgot... the half-painted background:

Some glyphs might overflow from their desired cell. Even with standard English text, some slightly antialiased pixels of the letters `m` or `w` might slightly overflow to the right.

With some other glyphs it's more extreme. E.g. a desert island + VS16 might be defined in the font as being way too wide. About twice as wide as the rest. And then it overflows.

An essential behavior of terminals is that the width is not dictated by the font. The width is dictated by other means, and in our example we believe the desired with is 1. That's why 1 cell is painted with blue background. The fact that the palm tree overflows to the right, by quite a lot, potentially overlapping with another glyph which just happens to be a space in your example, is an unrelated story, and does not cause the background to be extended.

It's arguable whether the font is erroneous for having overly large glyphs, or whether VTE should center the glyph horizontally (i.e. overflowing by about half a cell in both directions), or shrink to fit in its desired width (or at least not to overflow that much) (probably this latter, it just hasn't been implemented yet).

I hope this makes sense.

---

I'd also point out that tmux is clearly aware that this character does not have width 2: why else would it emit a `CUP` to column 41 after this character and before printing the remaining characters, to jump to the column that _would_ already be the current column if the character _had_ width 2.

---
Great observation; but then why doesn't it just simply emit a space if it knows that the width is 1?

Maybe because it's aware of the ambiguity, it knows that it doesn't know the behavior of the terminal underneath, and wishes to implement the "width 2" behavior over either behavior provided by the host.

But (if I'm right with this assumption) it fails to take the nondefault background color into consideration while implementing this logic.

No, this is not quite correct. The reason for both the backspace and the CUP is that tmux only knows the emoji is width 2 when it sees the VS16, up until that point it is width 1.

The third line of the `t.txt` file shows how tmux redraws the line again when it already knows about the VS16 and doesn't need to adjust the width. In this case, it does not need to make changes so there is no backspace or CUP.

It seems from all this that the fact is that VTE simply does not yet support Unicode 14 where these characters are width 2 with VS16. If they are currently drawing the character as width 1, then they are right that they only need to fill in the background of one cell - and indeed there is nothing to fix; only if they are drawing it as width 2 do they need to fill the background of both cells. The reason for my confusion is that your first screenshot (which I believed was VTE) showed the character as width 2.

You can see how the width changes with VS16 in WezTerm with Unicode 14:
![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d8547ec9-e573-4794-94e5-883cc8bd948e)

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
tmux's idea of character width, the terminal's and the application's must all match or there will be drawing errors. This is what is happening here and is a common problem because there is a big range of libc, terminal and application support for Unicode. It especially shows up with emojis.

It is unfortunately hard for any application, including tmux, to work out what the terminal supports, so we have to make a choice. At the moment, we have chosen to support this behaviour, which right now is only available in newer terminals. This is firstly on the (perhaps specious) grounds that the kind of user who wants to use the very newest emojis is going to be one who is happy to also use the very newest terminals; and secondly that eventually most active terminals will support this whereas none will move back from new to old behaviour.

Someone did suggest looking for 2027 with DECRQM, so we could try that...

We should perhaps also send iTerm2's OSC 1337 UnicodeVersion extension sequence, although I'm not sure how we could decide whether to send it or not.

comments.author: participant1

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
From https://<redacted-host>/GNOME/vte/-/issues/2878:

> Unicode 14 where these characters are width 2 with VS16

A link to the relevant part of Unicode would be highly appreciated, as I currently don't have time, nor motivation to thoroughly go through every aspect of Unicode, and the first page of web search results didn't give me anything relevant.
Let's assume that Unicode indeed states that VS16 in terminals should make some (or all?) characters double wide. My questions then:


* Does it apply to the input processing component, just like combining accents? I.e. they form an unseparable cell-pair, dragging the base character to the next line if necessary, and overwriting any of the two cells would erase the other half as well? Is it okay to ignore VS16 if there's anything else (e.g. color changing or cursor moving escape sequence) in between? Or, alternatively, (way less preferred approach by me) does each the base character as well as VS16 live their own lives, each in a single cell, subject to be overwritten separately, and it's the displaying part's responsibility to combine them, even across a linebreak?

* Do we need to support VS15 as well, which (as far as I know) picks the narrow variant even if the base character is wide? If so, how to handle line breaks? A wide base character doesn't fit in the very last cell, so wraps to the next line, causing the entire contents to scroll. A bit later VS15 arrives, and now we know that the character would have fit in the previous line and we shouldn't have scrolled. What to do?

* Any other special cases we need to be aware of? Triple, quadruple widths maybe?

* Did Unicode realize that they broke `wcwidth()`, `wcswidth()` and presumably quite some other APIs, and in turn the look of many-many apps out there? What have they done to mitigate or eliminate this breakage? What plan do they have to make this jump happen across this breakage?

* Where is the official source of which characters need to be widened with VS16? (Also, I'm wondering, is there a glibc, glib or any other API available for that, or do we have to work from the raw Unicode data files?)


If Unicode indeed states that VS16 makes characters wider then I'm afraid they introduced a heavily backwards-incompatible change, and whereas I understand that both you and tmux's developer wish to already "get to the other side", disregarding (or living with) those plenty of breakages that you see across a plethora of apps, I have a strong feeling that the vast majority of the terminal world is still on the "old" side. The majority of terminals that I have on my system and could quickly check, plus ncurses (which a lot of terminal-based apps build upon), at least.

> [ncim over there] tmux's idea of character width, the terminal's and the application's must all match or there will be drawing errors. This is what is happening here and is a common problem because there is a big range of libc, terminal and application support for Unicode. It especially shows up with emojis.

This is absolutely true. Unicode folks coming up with a backwards incompatible change, and *some* software (in the name of claiming to be *modern*) jumping on it and implementing that change, is not the right approach in my opinion. At the very least, whoever decided that this change is desired, should have come up with an escape sequence to switch back and forth, or some other migration plan.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
I can't say I care that much for reading about emojis in Unicode either, but it looks like the thought process is that VS16 mandates "emoji presentation" and given that, the guideline is that they should be square which means width 2, probably this text from https://unicode.org/reports/tr51/:

> Current practice is for emoji to have a square aspect ratio, deriving from their origin in Japanese. For interoperability, it is recommended that this practice be continued with current and future emoji.

I don't much like it myself, but this is what the terminals that support this are doing and I won't be able to change it even if I was inclined to try (which I'm not).

From tmux's perspective I don't know of a sensible way to figure out what the terminal will do and so far most of the people who care about these characters have cared about them working the new way rather than the old.

I'll think about whether a terminfo capability to specify VS16 behaviour would be sensible or if this is just something we should live with until it settles one way or another.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
I asked at https://<redacted-host>/pipermail/unicode/2025-April/011424.html for clarifications if Unicode emojis should allocate one or two columns when presented with monospaced fonts.

The reply from https://<redacted-host>/pipermail/unicode/2025-April/011426.html says: it depends on the emoji, the Unicode file EastAsianWidth.txt gives the width of each character; one will see there that some Emoji are full-width characters (take 2 columns) while others are half-width (take 1 column).  The Variation Selector doesn't (or shouldn't) change that.

https://<redacted-host>/Public/16.0.0/ucd/EastAsianWidth.txt contains:

> 1F3D4..1F3DF   ; N  # So    [12] SNOW CAPPED MOUNTAIN..STADIUM
> 
> 1F3CF..1F3D3   ; W  # So     [5] CRICKET BAT AND BALL..TABLE TENNIS PADDLE AND BALL

The terms in the second column "A", "F", "H", "N", "Na", and "W" seem to be defined at https://<redacted-host>/reports/tr11/ .

"N" is Neutral - https://<redacted-host>/reports/tr11/#ED7 - 

> In a broad sense, wide characters include W, F, and A (when in East Asian context), and narrow characters include N, Na, H, and A (when not in East Asian context).
> 
> Narrow (and neutral) Unicode characters always map to regular (narrow) characters.

My reading is that Desert Island U+1F3DD is one column, while Table Tennis Paddle and Ball U+1F3D3 is two columns.

**Does this clarify all concerns?**

The patch `vs.diff.txt` with `set -s variation-selector-always-wide off` does work, but I think now there is a specification telling how wide each emoji should be.  So ideally this patch will not be necessary.

comments.body:
No, the issue with VTE was that *if* they display the character as width 2 (which your screenshot shows them doing), then they should draw the second cell that the character covers in the same background colour as the first (which your screenshot shows them not doing). But it turns out that they *intend* to treat this character as width 1, in which case they do not need to draw the second cell at all (because there isn't one), and the problem is simply that tmux and VTE disagree about the character widths, which is not uncommon. Unicode support between applications, terminals, fonts and system library implementations (that is, wcwidth) is all over the place, particularly for emojis.

I'm not getting any further into whether emojis with VS16 should be width 1 or 2 because it doesn't really matter what I think about it. Terminals supporting Unicode 14 are drawing them as width 2, we've already discussed a couple and there are more mentioned in https://github.com/tmux/tmux/issues/3923. The question is only what effort tmux should put into supporting terminals doing it the "old" way. That is, should it have an option to pick "new" or "old" behaviour (easy) or should it try to adapt to the outside terminal the way it does for many other features (harder).

I appreciate you are interested in this and want to follow it up but I'm not the person to talk to, and in my experience this stuff just ends up with everyone exchanging huge walls of text (like this one) and nothing happens.

If you want to discuss the right or wrongs of this, the best thing would be to try a few terminals which have this feature and 1) look for ways in which tmux does not work correctly with those terminals or where I have misunderstood what they are doing (make sure to configure them for Unicode 14 if needed) 2) or discuss with their developers whether the behaviour is right with respect to the Unicode specification.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
From https://<redacted-host>/GNOME/vte/-/issues/2878:

My understanding about the discrepancies between VTE/tmux is not whether emoji+VS16 is one/two columns width, but per https://github.com/tmux/tmux/issues/4475 and the screenshots I uploaded there:

> the issue with VTE was that if they display the character as width 2 (which your screenshot shows them doing), then they should draw the second cell that the character covers in the same background colour as the first (which your screenshot shows them not doing). But it turns out that they intend to treat this character as width 1, in which case they do not need to draw the second cell at all (because there isn't one), and the problem is simply that tmux and VTE disagree about the character widths, which is not uncommon. Unicode support between applications, terminals, fonts and system library implementations (that is, wcwidth) is all over the place, particularly for emojis.

Provided that VTE displays the character with double width, as demonstrated by a screenshot, can it draw also the second cell in the same background colour, or not draw the second cell at all?

---

Presumably every terminal emulator has two fundamentally different components: The emulation layer where it imagines in its mind which cell contains which character with what graphical attributes; and the display layer which implements this look.

In its emulation layer, VTE is clear: it obeys the `wcwidth()` and also EastAsianWidth data, and (as confirmed on the Unicode mailing list) a VS16 does *not* alter the width. E.g. Desert island + VS16 occupies a single cell. Any subsequent operation, e.g. positioning the cursor to a certain column and overwriting the data there, works according to this logic.

Now, when it comes to drawing, VTE first paints the background color of each cell, then it draws each glyph by aligning its left edge at the target cell's left edge. If a glyph overflows to the right then it overflows, VTE lets it overflow. In this specific case it overflows *by a lot*. (Or, if you happen to place it at the rightmost cell, then due to lack of space it gets cropped.) Call it a visual glitch in VTE if you will.

VTE could alter its strategy: could center the glyph horizontally, or crop, or shrink. That would change absolutely nothing with interoperability with Tmux or any other piece of software, because for those interoperability issues only the emulation behavior matters. If VTE and Tmux disagree on the desired logical emulation behavior (as they do now) then fine-tuning the painting algorithm won't be able to fix that.

The solution would not be super simple. Some letters slightly overflow to the right (maybe by just a fraction a pixel: some antialiased pixels) and this is absolutely legitime. Shrinking those letters to make them strictly fit would even make plain English text look bad, e.g. `m `or `w` would be smaller than the rest. A strategy should be carefully designed, implemented and thoroughly tested where e.g. shrinking only kicks in if the glyph would overflow *too much* (according to some fine-tuned parameters), or only certain glyphs (emojis) are subjected to shrinking, or such.

I'd love to see VTE shrinking these glyphs rather than overflowing by such extreme amounts, but again, it's not trivial to properly implement this, nor would fix any of the problems you have with Tmux.

Or we could just blame it on the font: a monospace font should really be monospace, respecting EastAsianWidth, throughout all its codepoints. But in practice these emojis are likely missing from the base font and substituted from another one.

---

> Provided that VTE displays the character with double width

We don't display it as double-width. We display it as wide as the font dictates. Which could be 1.1x width or 1.8x width or 2.1x width or whatever.

The next cell, into which the emoji overflows, could have its own background color and its own glyph (which clashes with the overflown parts of the emoji). It just so happens that in your examples you always print a space there (or skip that cell). Try printing a letter immediately after the emoji and you'll see the clash.

Extending the background is not an option. It would break the look of apps that extensively use background colors (think of e.g. mc, alsamixer) whenever a letter like `m` or `w` ever so slightly overflows to the next cell. Let alone the required code complexity and runtime penalty. The intruder, overflowing glyph should not be able to claim even more rights, and disregard the properties of the glyph that is really meant to be in that cell (even if that glyph happens to be a space).

Now, of course, you might decide to print a space character there with the same background as the one you used for your emoji. If Tmux wishes to implement the "width 2" strategy over a terminal that uses the "width 1" strategy then I believe this is what it should do.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
I've observed something that is likely relevant to this thread: tmux sometimes inserts a space in lines that have certain unicode characters. The easiest way to reproduce I've found:
```
tmux new
perl -le 'print "⚌".("a"x100) for 1..50' | less
```
This happens with tmux 3.5a.

Interestingly, when I execute the command without the less, it may or may not insert the space right after the ⚌ character (but then it does that consistently). With the less, it sometimes inserts the space in the middle of the line.

My prompt includes some fancy unicode characters, and I experience weird behavior when trying to edit the command line: tmux seems to insert a space right in the middle of a word I'm typing.

This behavior does seem to be related to character's width: this ⚌ (U+268C) character I'm using for the example looks to be single width in the monospace font I'm using in my terminal, but it's kinda double width here. There is no weirdness with characters like é or あ.
